parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3 Nf6
parent.overview: 4.c3 prepares d2-d4 so White can build a pawn pair on d4 and e4 with the bishops behind it, and it denies Black's knight d4. Black usually answers 4...Nf6. White then chooses between the classical 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ (7.Bd2 for a roughly equal game with Black's hanging pawns, or 7.Nc3, the Greco Gambit/Moller Attack, which is extremely sharp) and the slower Giuoco Pianissimo with 5.d3 and a later d4, which has been the preferred elite approach since the 1980s. The c3 pawn blocks the queen's knight, so it travels Nbd2-f1-g3. The branches differ greatly: the Pianissimo is a manoeuvring game, the 5.d4 and Moller lines are forcing and heavily analysed.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 dxc4 3. Nf3 Nf6
parent.overview: After 2...dxc4 Black has taken the c-pawn, but sources agree he cannot keep it without serious concessions; White regains it with Bxc4 once the e-pawn has moved (3.e3 or 3.Nf3 then e3, or 3.e4). Black instead gives up the idea of holding it and fights for central counterplay: ...c5 (and ...cxd4) or ...e5 to undermine d4, and ...a6 with ...b5 to gain queenside space and time for the c8 bishop. The centre is open, White has the d4/e4 pawns and the move, and the usual middlegames are IQP or hanging-pawn positions with piece play. Character varies by line: the 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bxc4 c5 main line is positional and balanced, while 3.e4 lines can be tactical early. It is sound and has been a regular at the elite level since the 1990s.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
parent.overview: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 is a crossroads, not one system: White develops the b1-knight before committing the c-pawn, which blocks White's own c-pawn and so gives up the usual c4 challenge to d5. The usual continuation is 2...Nf6, after which White chooses between 3.Bg5 (Richter-Veresov: pin on f6, queenside castling, f3 and e4) and 3.Bf4 (Jobava London: Nb5 ideas against c7, Qd2 and Bh6 against a fianchetto), or 3.Nf3 and transpositions. Other Black replies are 2...Bf5 (Alburt Defence, assessed as equal, rare in master play), 2...c5 (Irish Gambit, little explored) and 2...e6. The openings are rarely used by top players as a main weapon but are sound; Spassky, Tal, Karpov, Bronstein, Morozevich, Aronian and Gashimov have played them as surprise weapons. The subtree also swallows a different opening by transposition: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6 is the Chigorin Defence, Black's choice, not White's.

parent.name: King's Indian Attack
parent.overview: White builds the mirror image of the King's Indian Defence: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and e4, usually against any Black set-up, particularly ...d5 with ...e6 or ...c5. The central pawn push e4-e5 gives a kingside bind and space, after which White expands with h4-h5, g4 and knight manoeuvres (Nf1-e3/g3 or Ne1-g2) towards a kingside attack. Black generally seeks counterplay on the queenside with ...c5, ...b5 or ...a5, or contests e4 directly. It has a modest theory load and keeps the same ideas whatever Black plays, so it is popular at club level, though it is uncommon among top grandmasters today. Black's main dilemma is that passive play lets White have a superior version of the King's Indian Defence, while ...e5 can leave Black behind in development.

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.
